concepts.def: y = aˣ with a > 0, a ≠ 1. Grows rapidly if a > 1; decays if 0 < a < 1. Always passes through (0, 1).
y = eˣ where e ≈ 2.71828. Unique property: d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ. Used for continuous growth/decay.
logₐ x is the inverse of aˣ: logₐ x = y ⟺ aʸ = x. Natural log: ln x = logₑ x.
log(xy) = log x + log y; log(x/y) = log x − log y; log(xⁿ) = n log x. Same base throughout.
logₐ x = logᵦ x / logᵦ a. Useful when calculator only has log₁₀ or ln.
Population growth, radioactive decay, Newton's law of cooling: all use y = Aeᵏᵗ. Log transforms linearise data.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Exponentials & Logarithms — a core area of A-Level Maths.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Exponentials & Logarithms brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Exponentials & Logarithms.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: If the dot product of two non-zero vectors is zero, what does that mean?
options: Definite integrals are negative only when the limits are reversed.
The vectors are perpendicular to each other.
It means at least one of the vectors is the zero vector.
It means the vectors are parallel.

mcqs.q: Can a definite integral give a negative value, even when integrating a function from left to right?
options: Definite integrals are always positive because area cannot be negative.
Yes — if the function is below the x-axis over the interval, the integral is negative.
Pick any point on the line — they're all equivalent.
Definite integrals are negative only when the limits are reversed.

mcqs.q: How do you use a conversion graph between miles and kilometres?
options: Look only at the gradient of the line and apply it as a formula.
Definite integrals are negative only when the limits are reversed.
Pick any point on the line — they're all equivalent.
Find the known value on its axis, draw a line to the graph, then read across (or down) to the other axis.
